title: When you're ill
hookLine: sickness is not punishment; Jesus healed the sick
tomorrow: Abuela's hands have hurt for years. why did nobody know?

lines: A FEVER, THIS WEEK OF ALL WEEKS.
cards: A fever, the very week you were supposed to shine. Lying on the couch, it's tempting to do the math: what did I do to deserve this? Skipped something, said something, owed somebody?
Jesus's own friends did that math out loud, about a man born blind. And Jesus refused to show his work their way.

teach.b: John tells it. The disciples see the man and ask, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rabbi, who hath sinned, this man, or his parents, that he should be born blind?" Two choices, both blame.
Jesus picks neither: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents; but that the works of God should be made manifest in him."

Then he spits on the ground, makes clay, puts it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash. One to tell a friend: the pool is called Siloe, and John stops to tell you the name means sent. The man comes back seeing.

So the Church keeps a sacrament just for the sick, the anointing of the sick, from the letter of James: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him."
It's a place where God's works can still show up, through healing, through a doctor, through the people on the couch beside you.
And every day of last week still holds when you're ill: a remembered day, a first birthday, a few days apart.

how: Catholics pray for the sick by name at Mass and at home; a priest can give the anointing of the sick to someone seriously ill, at home, in a hospital or in church.

o: a sign that someone has sinned and is being punished
a time of sickness, met as a place God still works
a reason to stop praying until you feel better

games.q: this week's lines, and today's — tap the pairs.
p: neither this man nor his parents
call the priests to pray over the sick

s: in John 9, the disciples assume someone's sin caused the blindness
who hath sinned, this man, or his parents? Jesus answers: neither.
Church law today requires a saint's name at baptism
back from this week: the current code only rules out names foreign to Christian sense.
a Catholic retreat and the Jewish Sabbath are the same thing with two names
back from yesterday: both make stopping holy, but the Sabbath is a weekly commandment.

games.q: your little brother overhears that a neighbor has cancer and whispers, 'is it because he stopped going to church?' what fits John 9?
o: no. Jesus said sickness isn't a punishment. we can pray for him.
maybe. sometimes God sends illness to make people come back.
we can't know, so it's better not to talk about it.
games.why: asked who sinned, Jesus answered neither, and then he healed. illness isn't a scorecard; it's a place to help and pray.

practice: Put one hand over a place that hurts or feels tired, or over your heart if nothing does. Breathe slowly there, and let the question of blame go quiet.
If you pray, you can pray for your own health, plainly, the way you'd ask for anything you need.

wordCard.voice: When you're ill. The time Catholics are taught to meet not as a punishment but as a place God can still work. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: weakness, sickness. the New Testament's ordinary word for being ill.

carryVoice: Keep this one: not a punishment, neither this man nor his parents. Get some rest.
